title: Ergo, free notes, and the form
introduction: This week's session was about the Ergo document and how it fits with the creative project design. The speaker explained how the two relate, and gave practical advice on filling in the forms without getting stuck.
related_work:
The Ergo document and the creative project design are not separate jobs. The Ergo requirements — background, industry practice and context, research questions, research design — all map onto the creative project design. The Ergo document is really a condensed version of the project writing: you submit both, and they should complement rather than repeat each other. The closing stage of the document also links back to the earlier points and the methods section, especially through the research questions.

The forms add their own constraint: the deliverable sections are small, and a downloaded form like form 102 has a fixed section 3 that you just apply. The advice was a free-notes method — for each question write down the first version that comes to mind, even a few words, and make sure every question is answered. The first pass is about breadth, not precision, because the real mistake is answering only part and leaving the rest blank.

For the research plan, if the research-question title is still uncertain, write a few keywords first, like '101 is to do such-and-such'. The research background just needs to explain why you are doing the research. The overall advice was to make the first pass fast — roughly three minutes — then move on and come back to revise, rather than getting stuck at the start. Titles and backgrounds can stay vague at first, with keywords and rough reasons as placeholders to be refined later.
